doc.title: Mr. and Mrs. A.C. Synigal Interview, 1962-05-24

title: Church at Ascension near Donaldsonville; no segregation then
summary: Buggy rides to Mass, her christening and communion at the old church, and the lack of segregation in those days.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: We, uh, well right out to Thibodeau. We'd go, my mother would drive us when I was a little girl, about 10 years old. We used to go to Thibodeau to Mass. And that's about 10 miles or something. Well, she'd have this horse on her. Well, it wasn't a, it wasn't a surrey. It was a buggy. Do you know what a buggy is? It was a buggy. Was she a buggy? No. Uh, she would, um, it was a buggy. My sister and I would have, uh, we'd sit on side when she, she'd have those, and it was, he was a race horse, this Diamond. My father had him as a race horse. And so she began to drive him. And used to drive him on Sunday morning, drive us to church. And here we were sitting on the side of her. And our curls, lulled curls would be just flying out. My mother would be holding, I can remember how she'd be holding the race horse, you know. And we'd get there in no time, uh, for these, uh, with this, with this race horse. Nobody couldn't drive him but my mother. And we used to go to church on Sunday morning. And go to, we used to go to school. We had one of those carriages, surrey's there, with the fringe on it. We used to go to school in that. Um, to Donisonville. That was a mile and a half.
Which direction is the plantation home from? Donisonville?

That's all, that's all, that's out from Tibidon. A mile and a half? Yeah. That's a, for instance, you cross the U.P. Long Bridge, you know. Oh yeah. And get that, keep you all the way going to Tibidon. And you wouldn't turn left, continue right. On the bayou.

Yeah, on the bayou. On the bayou. On that bayou. Bayou Lafour. On that road. On that road. Continue on that bayou Lafour. A mile and a half from Donisonville. Donisonville. On bayou Lafour. And you can't miss it because that great big Catholic church is there. Noted, oh, it's been there over a hundred years. Since, what, St. uh, the Ascension. The Ascension. The Ascension. The Catholic church. There where I was christened there. And, uh, made my communion there. That big church. And in those days, now, I don't want to talk politics and anything like that. But in those days, we had no segregation. I made my communion. Thanks to white girls. Well, it's far different in those days from these days. I was at the Holy Family. I came to the Holy Family Convent here during my retreat. Because one of the sisters from out there came. And he used to take us, everybody brought me here. And then that Saturday evening, we went back home. And made my communion that Sunday morning. And, um, I, when my children, when I take my children out there, I show them the seat I was sitting in. And don't you know they know it when we go now, the smallest one. This is where my mayor used to sit when she made her communion. And they handed it all the way down. Everybody knows it now. So, uh, and well, those are nice things to remember, you know. And, uh, I remember when there's no segregation at all. I know you all, you don't remember. Of course, you were too young. I'm sure both of you. But when I was a little girl, about ten years old, Tim, we lived in the country and I came here. We used to come off first. We came here often. And, uh, I remember, um, wait, we moved here. When we moved here, we moved on a boat. Now, I can't, that's one thing I can't remember, is the boat we moved on. Remember they had those boats coming back and forth? We moved here on a boat. Now, I can't remember which boat. If they called the names of the boat, maybe I could remember that. So, we had to get the Espinade. We got down on Espinade Wharf. Espinade and the river. We got down on the bus. And we got the Espinade car. I know whether the wagon or truck or something took the furniture. But we got on the street car. There was no buses then. Got on the street car and that's one thing I can remember as a child. Well, my brothers and sisters, they hardly came, but I would always come with my aunt and everything. And I got in the street car and ran all the way to the front seat. All the way to the front seat. Now, I can remember it just as plain as today. And I was a child then. So, when I tell that to people, they said, older people than me, they said, well, you're telling the truth. There was no segregation there. There really was no segregation there. That's what I heard. It was the truth. It was the truth. I did it. I know. That's one thing I remember doing myself. And I told them, I said, I'm sure I'm not imagining that. I said, I did that. I said, yes, you did. I asked the old people about it. And they said, sure, there was no segregation there. It's just recently in about, how many years? About 30? Less than?
You think that's how old? Oh, yeah.
Probably back from 1900. I didn't remember.
